questions.q: What does sysctl actually control, and how does it differ from a filesystem-permission check in a CIS Benchmark?
options: It reads and writes kernel parameters live through /proc/sys/, operating at a layer below filesystem permissions and services
It is identical to a CIS Benchmark scanner and performs the same function
It is a GUI tool for configuring desktop wallpaper settings
It only manages which users are allowed to log in over SSH
questions.explain: sysctl controls kernel-level behavior such as networking, crash dump behavior, and memory address exposure — a layer below file permissions and service configuration.

questions.q: Why should net.ipv4.ip_forward be set to 0 on a host that isn't acting as a router?
options: Because it disables all networking on the host entirely
Because it is required for SSH to function correctly
So the kernel won't forward packets between network interfaces, preventing a compromised host from being repurposed to pivot traffic between network segments
Because it has no security implication and is purely cosmetic
questions.explain: ip_forward controls whether the kernel forwards packets between interfaces; leaving it enabled unnecessarily gives an attacker a way to pivot traffic.

questions.q: What risk does setting fs.suid_dumpable to 0 address?
options: A crashed setuid program could otherwise write a core dump containing sensitive memory, including credentials, to a file a less-privileged user might read
It disables sudo entirely so no setuid programs can run
It has no real security purpose and is purely for disk space savings
It prevents any program on the system from ever crashing
questions.explain: Setuid programs run with elevated privileges; a core dump from one left at default settings can leak sensitive in-memory data to an unprivileged reader.

questions.q: What attack does enabling net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies defend against?
options: A SQL injection attack against a web application
A brute-force password-guessing attack against SSH
A phishing email containing a malicious attachment
A SYN flood denial-of-service attack, where an attacker opens huge numbers of half-finished TCP connections to exhaust the server's connection table
questions.explain: SYN cookies let the kernel verify a connection is legitimate without holding state for it until the handshake completes, defeating SYN flood exhaustion attacks.

questions.q: Why does hardening work need to end up in a file under /etc/sysctl.d/ rather than just a sysctl -w command at the terminal?
options: sysctl -w commands are purely cosmetic and never actually change kernel behavior
A sysctl -w change takes effect immediately but is lost on the next reboot, while files under /etc/sysctl.d/ are re-applied automatically on every boot
There is no practical difference between the two approaches
/etc/sysctl.d/ files only work on systems that have never been rebooted
questions.explain: A one-off sysctl -w disappears at reboot. Drop-in files under /etc/sysctl.d/ (applied via sysctl --system) are the durable, boot-persistent way to set a parameter.
